title: Number of Ways to Split Array
description: Brute force to optimized: resumming both sides at every index versus a running left sum with an algebraically derived right sum.

content.title: Number of Ways to Split Array

blocks.text: Given a 0-indexed integer array nums of length n, an index i (with i + 1 less than n) is a valid split if the sum of the first i + 1 elements is greater than or equal to the sum of the remaining elements. Return the total number of valid split indices.

blocks.caption: Track a running left sum and derive the right sum from the total, counting every valid split

blocks.text: Given a 0-indexed integer array nums of length n, an index i (with i + 1 less than n) is a valid split if the sum of the first i + 1 elements is greater than or equal to the sum of the remaining elements. Return the total number of valid split indices.

blocks.title: Analogy: Splitting a Bill Fairly, or Unfairly, Between Two Groups
blocks.text: Like sliding a divider along a line of people each holding a different amount of money, counting every position where the group on the left is holding at least as much total money as the group on the right.

blocks.caption: Slide the divider one position at a time, counting every point where the left side still leads

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["i=0: left=10, right=4+(-8)+7=3, 10 >= 3","valid split","The first element alone already outweighs everything remaining"],["i=1: left=10+4=14, right=-8+7=-1, 14 >= -1","valid split","Adding the second element grows the left side even further ahead"],["i=2: left=14+(-8)=6, right=7, 6 < 7","not valid","The left side has fallen behind the single remaining element on the right"],["Answer","2","Exactly 2 of the 3 possible split points satisfy the condition"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["i=0: left=2, right=3+1+0=4, 2 < 4","not valid","The left side does not yet outweigh the rest of the array"],["i=1: left=5, right=1, 5 >= 1","valid split","The left side has now pulled ahead"],["i=2: left=6, right=0, 6 >= 0","valid split","With only one element remaining on the right, the left side easily leads"],["Answer","2","2 of the 3 possible split points are valid"]]}

blocks.text: With only two elements, the only possible split point is i = 0, giving left = 1 and right = 1; since 1 is greater than or equal to 1, this is a valid split, so the answer is 1.

Before summing both sides independently at every candidate split, notice this is structurally the exact same relationship exploited in Find Pivot Index: left plus right always equals a fixed total, so only one side ever truly needs to be tracked.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any split index i, leftSum(i) plus rightSum(i) always equals the total sum of the entire array, since together they cover every element exactly once with nothing left out and nothing double-counted.

Observation 2: This means rightSum(i) is always recoverable as total minus leftSum(i), with no need to separately scan or sum the right portion at all, for any candidate split point.

Observation 3: leftSum(i) can be built incrementally while scanning left to right, growing by exactly one element at each step, the same running-total idea used throughout every prefix sum problem.

Observation 4: So a single left-to-right pass, maintaining only the running leftSum and the once-computed total, is enough to check the validity condition at every candidate split point in O(1) work each, simply comparing leftSum against total minus leftSum.

Whenever a problem compares a growing left-side aggregate against a shrinking right-side aggregate across every possible split point, track only the running left side and derive the right side from a known total, exactly the same trick that works whenever left plus right always sums to something fixed.

The only real difference from Find Pivot Index is that this problem counts every index satisfying an inequality, rather than searching for the first index satisfying an equality, so the scan continues all the way through instead of stopping early.
For every candidate split index, separately sum the elements to its left, inclusive, and the elements to its right, and compare the two sums directly.

items: For each index i from 0 to n minus 2, sum nums[0] through nums[i] for the left sum.
Sum nums[i plus 1] through the end for the right sum.
If the left sum is greater than or equal to the right sum, count this as a valid split.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop only runs up to n minus 2, never reaching the very last index, since a valid split explicitly requires at least one element remaining on the right side.
The left sum includes index i itself, since the split condition explicitly defines the left side as the first i plus 1 elements.
count is incremented, not overwritten, for every valid split found, since the problem asks for the total number of valid splits, not just whether one exists.

blocks.text: Every candidate split index's true left and right sums are directly computed and compared, so the correct total count of valid splits is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each candidate index re-sums up to n elements across both sides.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the recomputation cost itself.

Limitation: leftSum(i) and rightSum(i) can both be derived from the total sum of the array and a single running left sum, without ever re-scanning either side from scratch, exactly as in Find Pivot Index.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force treats the left and right sums at every candidate index as two entirely fresh calculations, but both are tightly constrained by one simple fact: together, they must always add up to the same fixed total sum of the array. That constraint means the right sum was never actually independent information at all, it was always fully determined the moment the left sum was known. Maintaining just one running quantity, the left sum, incrementally as the array is scanned, and deriving the right sum algebraically at each step, replaces two separate O(n) scans per candidate index with two O(1) operations, a single subtraction and a single comparison, continuing across the entire array instead of stopping at the first match.

Compute the total sum of the array once, up front. Then scan left to right, growing a running leftSum by one element at a time. At each candidate split index, the right sum is simply total minus leftSum, so the validity condition can be checked with a single comparison, and every valid split is counted directly.
Grow a running left sum while scanning once, deriving the right sum algebraically and counting every valid split.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to find the total, one pass to check and count every candidate index.
Space: O(1) extra.

Since leftSum(i) plus rightSum(i) always equals the fixed total sum of the array, rightSum(i) is always exactly total minus leftSum(i), a direct algebraic consequence holding at every candidate index without needing separate verification. Because leftSum only ever grows by exactly one element per step, and always represents the true sum of the first i plus 1 elements at the moment it is checked, the derived rightSum is always correct too, and the comparison against it correctly identifies every valid split.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","How it is obtained"],"rows":[["leftSum at index i","Maintained incrementally, growing by nums[i] at each step before the comparison"],["rightSum at index i","Derived algebraically as total minus leftSum at i, never scanned directly"]]}

items: total is computed once, in a single pass, before the main scanning loop begins.
leftSum is updated by adding nums[i] before the comparison at index i, since the split condition explicitly includes index i itself as part of the left side.
The loop only checks indices up to n minus 2, correctly stopping before the very last index, since a valid split always requires at least one element remaining on the right.
count is incremented, never reset or overwritten, every time the condition holds, correctly accumulating the total number of valid splits across the entire single pass.

blocks.text: This problem is a direct, count-based sibling of Find Pivot Index: the same total-minus-running-left-sum technique applies unchanged, just checking an inequality instead of an equality, and tallying every match instead of stopping at the first.

items: Forgetting that a valid split explicitly requires at least one element remaining on the right side, and allowing the loop to check the very last index, which has no right side at all.
Updating leftSum after the comparison instead of before, which would incorrectly exclude the current index's own element from its own left sum.

Returning the first valid split found, as in Find Pivot Index, instead of counting every one of them, conflating this problem's counting requirement with a different, similar-looking search requirement.

items: Explicitly connect this problem to Find Pivot Index out loud, since recognizing that the same total-minus-running-sum technique applies, just with a different comparison and a count instead of an index, demonstrates real pattern transfer rather than solving each problem from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count how many split points satisfy some left-side-versus-right-side comparison" points toward the total-minus-running-left-sum technique, exactly like Find Pivot Index, but tallying every match across the full scan instead of stopping at the first.

items: How would you find the split point that gives the largest difference between the two sides, instead of counting valid ones? Track the best, largest or smallest, difference seen during the same single pass, updating it alongside the running leftSum, instead of incrementing a counter.

What if "valid" meant the two sides had to be exactly equal instead of left greater than or equal to right? This becomes exactly the Find Pivot Index problem, just phrased in terms of splitting rather than finding a single balancing index.

How would this scale if nums could be updated between queries asking for the current count of valid splits? A plain running sum breaks down under updates; a Fenwick tree could maintain prefix sums efficiently, though re-deriving the full count of valid splits after an update would still require more care than a single O(log n) point update.

Direct sibling of Find Pivot Index, sharing the identical total-minus-running-left-sum technique, just swapping equality for a greater-than-or-equal comparison and swapping "find the first" for "count every one".
Same single running accumulator technique as Running Sum of 1d Array and Find the Highest Altitude, just paired here with a counting condition instead of building an array or tracking a maximum.
Same "total sum minus a running one-sided total" trick reused throughout prefix-sum problems whenever both a left and a right aggregate are needed simultaneously.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (running leftSum, derived rightSum): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Running left sum with an algebraically derived right sum, counting every index where the split condition holds
Core Idea: Since leftSum plus rightSum always equals the fixed total, only leftSum needs to be tracked; rightSum is always total minus leftSum, letting every split point be checked in O(1)
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The same total-minus-known trick behind Find Pivot Index applies directly here, just counting every match across a full scan instead of returning the first one
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium
One-line memory trick: leftSum grows, rightSum is just total minus leftSum; count every point where left still leads
